idiom_name: std::function handler table keyed by the message discriminator (or std::variant + std::visit)
implementation_notes: The standard library ships no router, so the C++ realization is a table the developer writes: a map from the message's discriminator to a std::function handler, with the rules as rows and an explicit fallback entry, which replaces the classic router-object hierarchy with one container. Prefer std::function when handlers are heterogeneous and the rules live at runtime; use plain function pointers or member-function pointers when they do not, because std::function allocates once its capture exceeds the small-buffer budget and copies the callable into every entry. Choose this form for value-based or configuration-driven rules; the C++17 variant/visit form below is the compile-checked alternative for a closed message set, and a per-destination stateful policy table is closer to a Dynamic Router.
pitfalls: std::function copies its callable into the table: a lambda capturing a large object by value duplicates that object per entry, and copying the table copies every capture again.
A table whose handlers capture references to locals or to `this` dangles as soon as the captured object dies - the classic dangling-capture bug in a long-lived router.
unordered_map has no evaluation order: when several rules can match, use an ordered vector of rows and document first-match-wins instead of relying on hash order.

variants.name: Closed std::variant message type with exhaustive std::visit (C++17)
variants.idiom_name: std::variant<OrderCreated, InvoiceIssued> + std::visit with an overloaded visitor
variants.implementation_notes: Model the messages as one closed std::variant and route with std::visit: the visitor's overload set is the routing table, the compiler refuses a visitor that does not handle every alternative (a missing route becomes a build error), and no string discriminator is compared at runtime. This replaces both the router object and the runtime predicate table whenever the message set is closed and known at compile time; the trade-off is that a new message type is a compile-time change at every visit site, and configuration-driven or value-based rules are no longer expressible (that stays the table form above). Use the variant from the decode boundary onwards, or keep the wire discriminator only at the very edge.
pitfalls: std::visit gives exhaustiveness but no ordering: destinations shared by several alternatives are expressed in the visitor body, not by falling through a rule list.
A variant can become valueless_by_exception (a throwing move during emplace) and visit then throws std::bad_variant_access, so the decode boundary - not the router - must handle that state.
